title: K-D-Sh
hookLine: kadosh, kiddush, kiddushin (marriage): all mean set apart

cards: Under a wedding canopy, a groom holds out a plain ring. The bride offers her finger, and before witnesses he says one short sentence in Hebrew. The word at its heart is mekudeshet.

Now go back to the desert, where Moses is given plans for a tent of woven curtains and gold, with one line of purpose. In the King James words: "let them make me a sanctuary; that I may dwell among them."
The Hebrew for sanctuary is mikdash. A ring and a tent, from different worlds. Underneath, one root: kuf, dalet, shin.
You met kuf on its own a couple of weeks ago.

teach.b: K-D-Sh. Four ways in. First, the core.
Kadosh, holy, from this root, means set apart: marked off from the ordinary, for something more. Second, a place. The mikdash in the desert is a space marked off from the camp around it.

And notice the reason the verse gives: not the gold, not the curtains, but a purpose, that I may dwell among them. The Temple in Jerusalem is remembered by the same word, the Beit HaMikdash, the house of the holy place.
The Sabbath is a day set apart from the week, and on Friday night a cup of wine is lifted for kiddush, the words that mark where the week stops and the day of rest begins.
The root does in time what the sanctuary does in space: it draws a border and says this side is different.
Fourth, a person. A Jewish marriage begins with kiddushin.

In the traditional words, the groom tells the bride that with this ring she is mekudeshet to him: set apart for him. One person, chosen out of all others, and the choosing is what makes the bond holy. Place, time, person.
In this root, holiness isn't floating somewhere above life. It's made by marking a line around something and keeping it. Set apart doesn't mean locked away.
It means given a place of its own.

how: On Friday evening, Jewish families say kiddush over wine to set the Sabbath apart; a Jewish wedding begins with kiddushin, when the groom gives the bride a ring with a formula saying she is set apart for him; the sanctuary in Exodus, and later the Temple, is called by the same root: mikdash.

o: the root of kadosh: holy, set apart for a purpose
the root of kohen: a priest who serves at the altar
the root of kavod: honor, weight, importance

p: a sanctuary, a place set apart
said over wine for the Sabbath
the start of a Jewish marriage

s: the Hebrew word for sanctuary, mikdash, shares a root with kadosh
kuf, dalet, shin: a place set apart.
kiddush and kiddushin come from the same root as kadosh
in this root, holy means locked away from ordinary life
it means marked off, given a place of its own: a place, a day, a person.

games.q: under the wedding canopy, the groom gives the ring and says the bride is mekudeshet to him. what does that root say she is?
games.why: set apart. mekudeshet grows from k-d-sh, the root of kadosh, holy: one person, chosen out of all others.

practice: Choose one thing in the day ahead to mark off from the rest: a cup you'll drink slowly, ten minutes with your phone in another room, a meal without hurry, a conversation given your whole attention.
Sit and notice the line you've just drawn between it and everything around it. If you pray, you can ask that this one thing be set apart.

wordCard.voice: K-D-Sh. Kuf, dalet, shin: the root of kadosh, holy; mikdash, the sanctuary; kiddush, over the wine; and kiddushin, marriage. All set apart. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a sanctuary, a place set apart, from the root kuf, dalet, shin.

carryVoice: Your line: set apart. A ring, a tent, a cup of wine: one root. Until next time.
